summary.title: Build Your Own Shell using Rust
summary.one_liner: You learn how a shell works by incrementally building a small one in Rust, from reading a single command to supporting arguments, built-ins like cd and exit, and pipes.
takeaways: A shell reads a line from stdin, splits it into a command and arguments, and spawns the program as a child process.
Wrapping the read-spawn-wait steps in a loop lets the shell accept multiple commands, and calling wait keeps the prompt from appearing too early.
Some commands such as cd must be built into the shell because they change state inside the shell process itself.
Pipes are implemented by connecting one child's stdout to the next child's stdin using Stdio::piped and Stdio::from.
summary.summary: The author walks through writing a shell in Rust in small, incremental steps, with each step shown as a code listing. The steps cover reading input with stdin().read_line, running commands with Command::new, adding a prompt loop and waiting on child processes, and splitting input on whitespace to pass arguments. Later sections add the cd and exit built-ins, graceful handling of unknown commands, and basic pipe support. The post is a learning project, and the author notes that simplicity was favored over robustness; the full code is on GitHub.
